title: Camp 2 close
hook: Krishna takes the reins; the stories you now carry
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eve, the conches, and Arjuna's bow slipping from his hand. Your line was the night before. Did you let yourself feel it, then rest? Day seventy-seven.

Before the war, before the conches, there's a scene the Mahabharata tells almost like a joke. Arjuna and Duryodhana both go to Krishna to ask for his help in the coming war. Krishna is asleep. Duryodhana arrives first and sits proudly by his head. Arjuna comes in and sits quietly at his feet. Krishna wakes, and the first person he sees is Arjuna. So Krishna makes an offer. On one side, my whole army, a vast force of warriors. On the other side, me. Alone. And I won't lift a weapon in the war. Choose.
screen: `TWO COUSINS AT KRISHNA'S BED.` → `ONE AT HIS HEAD, ONE AT HIS FEET.` → `MY ARMY, OR ME, UNARMED.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, asked first, chooses Krishna. No army. Just him. Duryodhana can hardly believe his luck: he gets the army. And then Arjuna asks Krishna to do one thing: drive my chariot. So the one the Gita will reveal as God becomes a driver. In Sanskrit, a sarathi, the one who holds the reins. Krishna is still called Parthasarathi, the charioteer of Arjuna, and there are temples to him by that name. That's where Camp 2 ends: a frightened man sitting in a chariot, and the one holding the reins about to speak. Now look back at what you're carrying. Fifty-five stories. A boy made from earth guarding a door, and an elephant head. The broken tusk that finished the Mahabharata. A mouse carrying a god: vahana. A sweet that comes back to you: prasad. A baby grabbing at the sun, a leap across the sea, a burning tail, a mountain carried whole: sankat mochan. A king with no sons, a bow, fourteen years, sandals on a throne, the forest years: vanaprastha. A golden deer. Lakshmana rekha. An old bird who tried. Shabari's berries. A squirrel on Rama Setu. A foot nobody could lift. Ten heads, a hymn to the sun, a queen's grief. Agni pariksha, the scene we didn't tidy up. Diwali, the lamps. And then cousins, dice, a cloth that wouldn't end, five villages, and the eve. Here's the point of all of it. When someone mentions Hanuman now, or Draupadi, or Bharata's sandals, you won't nod politely. You'll know. You know these people now. Next, the practices, the things these stories were pointing at all along. And when a festival's date arrives, its story comes first. Tomorrow: the night Krishna was born.
screen: `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA, UNARMED.` · `SARATHI: THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE REINS.` · `FIFTY-FIVE STORIES YOU CARRY.` · `YOU KNOW THESE PEOPLE NOW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Picture a chariot, and someone steady holding the reins. Now let the stories walk past, one at a time, like faces at a crowded station. Ganesha. Hanuman. Sita. Lakshmana. Jatayu. Shabari. Vibhishana. Mandodari. Draupadi. Arjuna. Don't try to remember everything. Just notice which face stops and looks at you. That's the one you're carrying out of this camp. Let it ride with you for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The driver. Sarathi, the one who holds the reins: Krishna, choosing to drive Arjuna's chariot instead of fighting.
Your line: you know these people now. Today, tell someone about the one character who stopped and looked at you. Camp 2 is done. Day seventy-seven.

screen: `DAY 77 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: JANMASHTAMI: THE NIGHT KRISHNA WAS BORN.`

howItsDone: Hindus also call Krishna Parthasarathi, Arjuna's charioteer, and the image of Krishna holding the reins while Arjuna listens is a familiar one in Hindu homes, in temples and on the covers of the Bhagavad Gita.
